mcqs.question: What must be true for decorators to be stackable in any combination?
options: Each decorator must know about every other decorator that might wrap the same object
Every decorator and the base object implement the same interface, so any decorator can wrap any other
The base object must be immutable
Decorators can only be applied to abstract classes, never concrete ones
mcqs.explanation: Shared interface is what makes nesting possible — a decorator wraps something implementing the interface and itself implements it too, so it's indistinguishable from the thing it wraps. Decorators don't need mutual awareness, immutability isn't required, and concrete classes work fine.

mcqs.question: You need to combine logging, retry, and caching behavior on a service call in different combinations depending on the caller. Why is Decorator generally a better fit here than a subclass per combination?
options: Decorator lets you compose behaviors at runtime instead of pre-defining one subclass for every combination
Subclassing is not supported in most modern languages
Decorators execute faster than any subclassed method
Decorator removes the need for a shared interface between the behaviors
mcqs.explanation: This is the subclass-explosion problem — N behaviors need up to 2^N subclasses to cover every combination, while decorators compose freely at runtime. Subclassing is fully supported everywhere; decorators aren't inherently faster; and a shared interface is required, not removed.

mcqs.question: A CachingImageLoader wraps a real ImageLoader and returns cached results without the caller knowing wrapping happened. A LoggingImageLoader wraps it to add a log line, and the caller deliberately chooses to add that layer. Which pattern is which?
options: Both are Decorator, since both hold a reference to the same interface
Both are Proxy, since both wrap an ImageLoader
CachingImageLoader is Decorator and LoggingImageLoader is Proxy
CachingImageLoader is Proxy (transparent optimization) and LoggingImageLoader is Decorator (deliberately added behavior)
mcqs.explanation: Proxy controls or optimizes access transparently — caching fits that. Decorator is a caller deliberately adding a new responsibility — logging, chosen and stacked on purpose, fits that. Structural similarity (both wrap the same interface) doesn't determine which pattern it is; intent does.

mcqs.question: Wrapping order is EncryptedStream(CompressedStream(file)) versus CompressedStream(EncryptedStream(file)). Why does this matter?
options: It doesn't matter — decorators are commutative by definition
The second form throws a runtime error in most languages
Compressing already-encrypted bytes barely compresses at all, since encrypted data looks like random noise
The first form is always slower because encryption is more CPU-intensive than compression
mcqs.explanation: Encrypted output is high-entropy, so a compressor finds almost no redundancy to exploit — order changes the actual outcome, not just performance. Neither ordering throws a runtime error, and relative CPU cost isn't the point being tested.
